heading: Can one effective complexity measure predict peaks across size, epochs and samples?
definition: the location of the peak along any axis (size, epochs, samples) is predicted by a single measure of effective model complexity.
summary: Independent studies in restricted settings support explanations based on spectra (patterns of eigenvalues or singular values), effective rank (the number of substantial directions) and model capacity, but a single predictor across model size, training duration and sample size remains contested. Counterexamples involving error over training challenge the universal explanation without directly measuring effective model complexity.

suggested_status.by_scale: Toy: R2 for restricted effective-rank and spectral accounts, with C for the universal epoch account. <1B: R2 for sample-axis capacity alignment only. Size-unspecified CNN/ResNet settings: C for the universal account. 1-10B: ? because the script bucket lacks clear parameter-scale confirmation in the displayed rows. 10-100B and >100B: ?; no coverage in the V5 size counts.
suggested_status.reason: The universal cross-axis statement is contested by the underparameterized epoch account (arXiv:2007.10099#R1) and the final-layer intervention (arXiv:2108.12006#r18), with the caveat that neither measures EMC. Low-noise ResNet18/CIFAR10 runs at widths k=64 and k=92 also challenge the authors' stated interpretation that the EMC hypothesis predicts epoch-wise double descent at all noise levels: no epoch-wise double descent occurs below noise fraction ε=0.025 (arXiv:2108.12006#r8; arXiv:2108.12006#r9). EMC and interpolation are not demonstrated for these particular low-noise runs. Independent restricted support includes size-axis spectral/rank associations (arXiv:2203.07337#r10-r15) and sample-axis capacity alignment in compact Transformers (arXiv:2505.24832#r1-r4). Relevant counts keys are versions.V5.verdicts, versions.V5.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original, versions.V5.studies_by_size and versions.V5.coverage_by_operation; these do not establish a shared predictor across axes.
suggested_status.open_questions: Would a prespecified, directly measured scalar locate peaks across size, epochs and samples in the same deep-network setting, with quantitative prediction errors? Would it correctly predict peak absence under final-layer convergence and low label noise, and retain accuracy across architectures, data geometry and training stages?

source.title: Deep double descent: where bigger models and more data hurt
source.authors: Preetum Nakkiran; Gal Kaplun; Yamini Bansal; Tristan Yang; B. Barak; I. Sutskever

original_result.setup: The original study varied model size, training duration and sample size in image and translation models.
original_result.result: With 15% label noise, sufficiently large ResNet18 models showed an error peak over training epochs near interpolation; data augmentation shifted the CNN peak across model sizes toward larger models. For Random Fourier Features, error peaked when the number of training samples equaled the feature dimension, but these observations did not establish a single predictor across model size, training duration and sample size.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: A Hessian-based count of influential directions tracked test-error curves and peaks in low-loss models.
Test-error peaks coincided with dips in the smallest positive eigenvalues of the features.
With and without augmentation, peaks followed each setting’s effective dimension: its count of influential directions.
Vanishing Hessian eigenvalues marked peaks; regression peaks followed effective rank, a count of influential directions.
Support vector regression peaks aligned at effective load 1 across error-tolerance settings.
More training samples shifted the MNIST RFM peak to larger widths.
Ridge regression peaked as α approached 1, while linear ESNs remained below that threshold.
Language-model transitions aligned near a dataset-to-capacity ratio of 1 across model sizes.
Boosting peaks tracked a complexity measure, with peak locations predicted more accurately after transforming input features.
Quantum kernel regression peaks matched predictions where normalized effective degrees of freedom approached 1.
Pretrained-regression peaks occurred when effective representation size matched the number of samples.
Portfolio risk peaked when dimension equaled sample count, whether varying dimension or sample count.
In several low-loss settings, log path-norm correlated at least as strongly as counts of influential dimensions.
Last-layer width determined the spectral drop, while earlier layers affected its magnitude.
Wide ResNet18 showed no epochwise double descent below label noise ε=0.025.
Counts of influential dimensions became unstable without risk peaks under random permutations or correlated noise.
In models with multiple components, changes in learning mechanism set peaks, sometimes before zero training error.
Training error missed ridge-model peaks; other models’ training-error minima coincided with their own peaks.
Bottleneck autoencoders retained a peak near d/n=1 despite being unable to interpolate.
Sparse-model peaks occurred when model size matched the number of observed coordinates.
A complexity estimate misplaced transitions in the eigenvalue spectrum and regression peaks on the original inputs.
Epochwise double descent occurred in underparameterized regression, challenging the effective-complexity explanation.
Bringing ResNet18’s final layer to convergence analytically eliminated epochwise double descent.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: A common, operationally fixed complexity measure quantitatively predicting peak locations across size, epochs and samples in the same deep-network setting.
untested.basis: The original's untested-parts line calls quantitative EMC prediction heuristic. Independent support uses axis-specific measures; the epoch challenges do not measure EMC. See arXiv:1912.02292#r2, arXiv:1912.02292#r17, arXiv:2003.02139#r8 and arXiv:2108.12006#r18. In CIFAR-100 ResNet18 width and CNN width/depth sweeps, effective-dimensionality correlations are restricted to training loss below 0.1; log path-norm correlates about as well or better, but peak-location prediction is not evaluated (arXiv:2003.02139#r10, arXiv:2003.02139#r11, arXiv:2003.02139#r12, arXiv:2003.02139#r13). These comparator correlations do not establish failure of V5, which does not require uniqueness. counts.versions.V5.main_rows_by_operation records operations, not validation of one measure across all axes.

untested.what: Peak-location prediction in models explicitly identified as 10–100B or >100B parameters.
untested.basis: counts.versions.V5.studies_by_size and counts.versions.V5.coverage_by_operation contain no 10-100B or >100B entries. Missing size metadata elsewhere cannot establish coverage.

untested.what: A validated common peak predictor across fine-tuned, instruct/chat and reasoning stages.
untested.basis: counts.versions.V5.studies_by_stage and coverage_by_operation.*.by_stage have no fine-tuned, instruct/chat or reasoning entries; the supplied tests do not compare a shared predictor across these stages.

untested.what: Validation of a common effective-complexity peak predictor under changes to earlier-layer bottlenecks.
untested.basis: arXiv:2107.12685#R7 and arXiv:2107.12685#R8 compare three-hidden-layer MNIST networks, including earlier bottleneck layers of width 10. The eigenvalue dip occurs when last-hidden-layer width reaches the training sample count; earlier layers affect dip magnitude and test error. The neural-network connection remains conjectural, and no bottleneck test-error peak is identified against which to evaluate prediction. These observations establish architectural dependence without demonstrating predictor failure. counts.versions.V5.main_rows_by_operation records operations, not validation across architectures.

untested.what: A common effective-complexity predictor explaining peak locations across the reported ridge, mixture-model and neural-network training-error associations.
untested.basis: arXiv:2305.14689, Appendix C, reports that ridge alignment-mismatch training error does not clearly signal the risk peak; a third-derivative minimum approximately tracks it. Section 5 and Appendix B report mixture-model and neural-network risk peaks coinciding with training-error minima. No single effective-complexity predictor is evaluated, and no corresponding V5 row is supplied. counts.versions.V5.main_rows_by_operation does not establish such validation.

untested.what: Validation of a unified effective-complexity peak predictor when exact interpolation is impossible in a bottlenecked linear denoising autoencoder.
untested.basis: arXiv:2505.24668, Section 5 and Figure 2, reports a peak near d/n≈1 for a two-layer linear denoising autoencoder with bottleneck width k below data rank r, despite impossible exact interpolation. Bottleneck width supplies an additional complexity measure, but no unified predictor is evaluated. This is a text-based finding without a corresponding V5 row. counts.versions.V5.main_rows_by_operation records operations, not validation of that predictor.

wording_issues.phrase: a single measure of effective model complexity
wording_issues.issue: Restricted size-axis evidence uses minimum-positive Hessian eigenvalues in MNIST1D networks; sample-axis alignment in GPT-style Transformers uses capacity measured in bits. A shared predictor across size, epochs and samples remains untested. The Transformer comparison's dataset attribution is internally inconsistent: Figure 3's caption says synthetic bitstrings, while Section 4 places it within FineWeb experiments.

For CIFAR-100 ResNet18 width and CNN width/depth sweeps restricted to training loss below 0.1, Hessian effective dimensionality tracks generalization curves and correlates with test outcomes; numerical peak-location prediction accuracy and prediction across size, epochs and sample count are not evaluated. The MNIST random-feature comparison reports qualitative movement of the width-axis peak with sample count without computing an effective-complexity measure. These findings leave V5 untested.

Epoch-wise evidence includes an analytic underparameterized counteraccount and a final-layer intervention eliminating the peak. These tests challenge the extension across axes, although neither computes EMC.

In oracle ridgeless regression with random-permutation augmentation, a pseudoinverse instability occurs without an additional risk peak. Predicting peak locations requires the risk-relevant matrix interaction beyond identifying a spectral instability.

method_sensitivity.what: Analytically converging the final layer eliminates epoch-wise double descent in the tested ResNet18 procedure. Standard SGD also shows no epoch-wise peak below noise fraction ε=0.025 at the tested wide settings. Section 8 interprets the EMC hypothesis as predicting epoch-wise double descent at all noise levels, making the low-noise absence a challenge under that interpretation. EMC is not measured, and interpolation is not demonstrated for those particular standard-SGD runs.

Rank-deficient correlated data place the unaugmented regression peak at d=2n; cropping and sign-flipping place the augmented peak at d=kn. Permutation augmentation separates the risk peak from a pseudoinverse instability.

In three-hidden-layer MNIST networks, earlier bottleneck layers of width 10 produce a sharper eigenvalue dip near last-hidden-layer width 1000 and higher test error. Earlier layers affect dip magnitude and test error. The text does not identify a bottleneck test-error peak whose location the eigenvalue predicts. These architectural observations provide coverage only: V5 is cannot_determine, with no demonstrated failure of the proposed spectral measure.

Changing where the sweep switches between parameter-increasing mechanisms moves or removes apparent peaks in regression trees, gradient boosting and random-feature regression. These experiments evaluate switch placement and interpolation without evaluating a single effective-complexity predictor of peak location. They provide coverage only for V5, whose state is cannot_determine; their V4 state is partial. The random-feature result also appears in Section 3.2, Figure 6(a).

The mean absolute spectral-transition offset from the nominal tree proxy crossing is 24.6 candidates on original covariates, 7.8 after Independentized transformation and 4.4 with unique ranks only. Feature permutation removes the regression signal, so the Independentized result is a geometry diagnostic on artificial data.

method_sensitivity.factor: Tree depth, training-set size and training duration
method_sensitivity.what: Deeper trees peak at smaller split-candidate count, while larger training sets peak at larger candidate count. Early boosting checkpoints lack a pronounced candidate-axis peak. These checkpoint comparisons do not establish an epoch-wise peak predictor.

In toy ε-SVR, peak locations align at effective load α̃=1 across ε=0.0,0.3,0.6,0.9. QKRR's effective-DOF account depends on ridge regularization, with the interpolation singularity analyzed in the small-ridge limit.
